subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: ‘The population grows at a rate proportional to its size.’ That sentence IS an equation — dP/dt = kP — and equations about rates are how science actually writes its laws. This unit teaches you to read them, check them, and solve them.
learning_objectives: Translate verbal rate statements into differential equations and back
Verify proposed solutions by substitution into the differential equation
Distinguish general solutions (families) from particular solutions (one curve)
Use initial conditions to select particular solutions
Identify equilibrium solutions where the derivative is identically zero

sections.title: Equations About Rates
sections.subtitle: Reading and writing the language
sections.body:
A differential equation (DE) relates a function to its own derivatives: dy/dx = x + y, dP/dt = kP, y'' = -y. Solving one means finding the FUNCTION(s) that make the equation true — a fundamentally different task from solving for a number, and the reason the subject feels new even though every tool involved is old.

Translation is the entry skill. 'Grows at a rate proportional to its size': dP/dt = kP. 'Cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the room's': dT/dt = -k(T - 70) (Newton's law of cooling — the minus encodes cooling toward the room). 'The rate of change of velocity is proportional to the square of speed, opposing motion': dv/dt = -kv². Each phrase maps to a derivative, a proportionality constant, and a sign chosen by physical direction.

The reverse reading matters equally: dy/dx = xy² says 'the slope of the solution curve at any point equals the product of the x-coordinate and the square of the y-coordinate.' A DE is a slope RECIPE — at every point of the plane it dictates the direction a solution passing through must head. That pointwise reading powers slope fields next chapter.

Sign conventions are graded: decay and cooling carry negative constants (or negative signs with positive k — state which), growth positive. The AP accepts either convention WHEN DECLARED; undeclared sign ambiguity in a model is where translation points die.
key_terms: An equation relating a function to its derivatives — solved by functions, not numbers
'Rate proportional to X' ⟹ derivative = k·X, sign by physical direction
A first-order DE assigns a slope to every point — the geometric meaning
boxes: ap_alert

Newton's law of cooling is the AP's favorite translation: dT/dt = -k(T - T_room) with k > 0. The rate depends on the temperature DIFFERENCE, not the temperature — writing dT/dt = -kT is the standard mistranslation and costs the modeling point.

sections.title: Verifying Solutions
sections.subtitle: Substitute and confirm both sides
sections.body:
Checking whether y = f(x) solves a DE requires no solving at all: compute the needed derivatives of f, substitute BOTH sides of the equation, and confirm identity. Does y = e^{3x} solve y' = 3y? Left side: y' = 3e^{3x}. Right side: 3y = 3e^{3x}. Equal for all x ✓ — it solves. Does y = x³ solve it? y' = 3x² versus 3y = 3x³: equal only at isolated points, not identically — no.

Verification questions are free points with a required format: compute the left side, compute the right side, state they match for all x in the domain. The AP asks 'verify that y = ... is a solution' as the opening part of DE FRQs regularly — it tests differentiation under a new costume and warms up the equation for later parts.

Families verify with the constant intact: y = Ce^{3x} solves y' = 3y for EVERY C (the C rides through both sides). Such a family is the GENERAL solution; choosing C via a known point gives a PARTICULAR solution. y(0) = 5 forces C = 5. The family-versus-member distinction organizes the whole unit: solving produces families; initial conditions pick members.

Implicit solutions verify by implicit differentiation: does x² + y² = C solve dy/dx = -x/y? Differentiate the relation: 2x + 2y y' = 0, so y' = -x/y ✓ — for every C at once. Unit 3's machinery, now certifying solution families it could not have named.
key_terms: Differentiate the candidate, substitute both sides, confirm identity for all x
The family with arbitrary constant(s): every member solves the DE
One family member, selected by an initial condition
boxes: ap_alert

Verification answers must show BOTH sides computed separately and then equated — 'y' = 3e^{3x} = 3y ✓' is the shape. Substituting the answer into itself or asserting equality without computing both sides earns nothing.

sections.title: Initial Conditions and Uniqueness
sections.subtitle: One point, one curve
sections.body:
An initial value problem (IVP) pairs a DE with a point: dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 4. The DE supplies the family; the point selects the member. Geometrically: through (almost) every point of the plane passes exactly one solution curve — the DE's slope recipe, integrated forward and backward from the anchor.

The constant-pinning workflow extends Unit 6's IVPs: find the general solution (by methods to come), substitute the initial point, solve for C, write the finished function. The exam's wrinkle: pin C at the RIGHT STAGE. When the general solution involves logs or exponentials of both sides, pinning C before exponentiating is usually cleaner — and chapter 4 makes this concrete.

Domain restrictions ride with particular solutions: y = 1/(1 - x) may solve y' = y² with y(0) = 1, but only on (-∞, 1) — the branch through the initial point, ending where the solution blows up. The AP asks for solution domains on occasion, and the rule is: the largest interval CONTAINING the initial point on which the solution is defined and differentiable. The other branch, however algebraically identical, is a different solution.

Equilibrium solutions are the constant members: values where the DE's right side vanishes identically. For dP/dt = 0.2P(10 - P): P = 0 and P = 10 are equilibria — start there and the system never moves. Equilibria organize the qualitative picture (solutions between 0 and 10 grow toward 10; above 10, decay toward it) and headline the logistic analysis two chapters ahead.
key_terms: DE + anchor point: the family narrowed to one curve
The largest interval around the initial point where the solution lives
Constant solutions where the rate is identically zero — the system at rest
boxes: ap_alert

'Find all values of P for which the population is not changing' means solve dP/dt = 0 — the equilibria. It is an algebra question hiding in a calculus unit, asked nearly every time a logistic or cooling model appears.

sections.title: Models Worth Knowing
sections.subtitle: The unit's recurring cast
sections.body:
Exponential growth/decay — dy/dt = ky: the rate is proportional to the amount. Money compounding continuously, radioactive decay, unchecked populations. Solution family (chapter 5 derives it): y = Ce^{kt}. The fingerprint: relative rate y'/y is CONSTANT.

Newton's cooling — dT/dt = -k(T - T_env): the rate is proportional to the gap from the environment. Coffee cooling, bodies in forensics, thermostats. Solutions decay exponentially TOWARD T_env rather than toward zero — a shifted exponential, with the equilibrium at room temperature.

Logistic growth — dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L): growth proportional to BOTH the population and the remaining room (L is the carrying capacity). Small populations grow almost exponentially; near capacity, growth chokes; the S-curve from Unit 5's epidemic example is this equation's solution. The BC exam's signature model, fully solved in chapter 6.

Reading model behavior WITHOUT solving is the unit's quiet superpower, available now: equilibria from the algebra (set the rate to zero), increasing/decreasing regions from the rate's sign, concavity from differentiating the DE itself (d²P/dt² via the chain rule on the right side). A surprising share of DE FRQ points require no solution formula at all — just Unit 5 analysis applied to the rate equation. The solving techniques ahead are for the parts that do.
key_terms: y' = ky: constant relative rate, family Ce^{kt}
T' = -k(T - T_env): exponential approach to the environment
P' = kP(1 - P/L): growth with a ceiling — BC's signature equation
boxes: ap_alert

Behavior questions ('is P increasing? concave up?') are answerable directly from the DE — substitute the value into the rate for the first, differentiate the DE (chain rule!) for the second. Reaching for the solution formula first is the slow road; the equation already knows.

mcq.question: 'The mass decays at a rate proportional to the mass present' translates to
mcq.explanation: Rate proportional to the amount, with decay's negative sign. (C is a solution, not the equation.)

mcq.question: Which function is a solution of y' = -2y?
mcq.explanation: y' = -14e^{-2x} = -2(7e^{-2x}) = -2y ✓ — and any constant multiple works.

mcq.question: The general solution of a DE is y = Ce^{x²}. If y(0) = 3, the particular solution is
The equilibrium solutions of dP/dt = 0.5P(8 - P) are
mcq.explanation: Set the rate to zero: 0.5P(8 - P) = 0 at P = 0, 8 — the constant solutions.

mcq.question: For dT/dt = -0.3(T - 20) with T(0) = 80, the temperature T is
mcq.explanation: At T = 80 the rate is -18 < 0: cooling. The rate vanishes at T = 20 — the environmental equilibrium the solution approaches.

frq.question:
Consider the differential equation dy/dx = 3y.
(a) Verify that y = Ce^{3x} is a solution for every constant C.
(b) Find the particular solution with y(0) = 5.
(c) Verify that y = 0 is also a solution, and explain its relationship to the family in (a).
rubric: (a) y' = 3Ce^{3x} and 3y = 3Ce^{3x}: equal for all x, any C
(b) 5 = Ce⁰ = C: y = 5e^{3x}
Relationship: the equilibrium, also the family member with C = 0
frq.model_answer: (a) Left side: y' = 3Ce^{3x}. Right side: 3y = 3Ce^{3x}. The two sides agree identically for every x and every C — the whole family solves the equation. (b) y(0) = C = 5: y = 5e^{3x}. (c) For y = 0: y' = 0 and 3y = 0 ✓. It is the equilibrium solution — the system at rest — and it belongs to the family as the C = 0 member, so the general solution y = Ce^{3x} already contains it.

frq.question:
A cup of coffee at 90°C sits in a 20°C room. Its temperature obeys dT/dt = -k(T - 20) for some k > 0, t in minutes.
(a) What does the model say about the SIGN of dT/dt while T > 20, and what does that mean physically?
(b) Without solving, find lim t→∞ T(t) and justify from the equation.
(c) Differentiate the DE to show d²T/dt² = k²(T - 20), and conclude the cooling curve is concave up while T > 20.
rubric: (a) T > 20 makes -(T - 20) < 0: dT/dt < 0, the coffee cools
(b) The rate vanishes only at T = 20 (equilibrium); cooling continues while above it: T → 20
(c) d²T/dt² = -k·dT/dt = -k·(-k(T - 20)) = k²(T - 20) > 0 for T > 20
Concavity conclusion: cooling fast at first, flattening toward the room temperature
frq.model_answer: (a) While T > 20, T - 20 > 0, so dT/dt = -k(T - 20) < 0: the temperature falls — hot coffee cools, as it must. (b) The only equilibrium is T = 20. The solution decreases while above 20 and its rate shrinks as the gap closes, so T(t) → 20 as t → ∞ — the coffee approaches room temperature without crossing it. (c) Differentiating both sides in t: d²T/dt² = -k(dT/dt) = -k(-k(T - 20)) = k²(T - 20). While T > 20 this is positive: the graph is concave up — steep cooling initially, leveling off as the cup nears the room's temperature, the familiar cooling-curve shape.

frq.question:
Let y = 1/(1 - x).
(a) Verify that y solves the differential equation dy/dx = y² with y(0) = 1.
(b) State the domain of this particular solution and explain why it stops where it does.
(c) The function z = 1/(1 - x) ALSO describes a curve for x > 1. Explain why that branch is NOT the solution to this IVP.
rubric: (b) Domain (-∞, 1): the branch through x = 0, ending at the vertical asymptote x = 1
(c) The x > 1 branch does not contain the initial point
A solution must live on one interval containing the anchor; disconnected branches are different solutions
frq.model_answer: (a) y' = d/dx (1 - x)^{-1} = (1 - x)^{-2} = [1/(1 - x)]² = y² ✓, and y(0) = 1/(1 - 0) = 1 ✓. (b) The solution's domain is (-∞, 1) — the largest interval containing the initial point x = 0 on which the formula is defined. The solution blows up at the vertical asymptote x = 1 (the curve escapes to infinity in finite x) and cannot be continued past it. (c) A solution to an IVP is a differentiable function on an INTERVAL through the initial point. The x > 1 branch never touches (0, 1) — it is a separate solution of the same DE (anchored by different conditions), not part of this one. Algebraic formulas can describe several solutions at once; the initial condition picks a single connected branch.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Slope Fields — Seeing Solutions Before Solving
hook: Draw a tiny dash at every point showing the slope the equation demands there, and solution curves appear like iron filings around a magnet. Slope fields let you SEE every solution at once — including the ones no formula can express.
learning_objectives: Construct slope field segments at given points from a differential equation
Match differential equations to slope fields by structural features
Sketch particular solutions through given points by following the field
Read equilibria, increasing/decreasing regions, and concavity from a field
Determine where slopes are zero, undefined, or constant along lines

sections.title: Building the Field
sections.subtitle: A dash at every point
sections.body:
A slope field (direction field) plots, at each grid point (x, y), a short segment with slope dy/dx as the DE dictates there. For dy/dx = x - y at the point (2, 1): slope 1 — a 45° dash. At (0, 2): slope -2 — steep downhill. The field is the DE made visible: every dash is one evaluation of the right-hand side.

Construction questions on the AP are exactly that mechanical: 'sketch the solution segments at the twelve indicated points' means twelve evaluations and twelve dashes with reasonable slopes (zero flat, ±1 at 45°, steeper distinguished from shallower). Precision to the degree is not graded; getting zero, sign, and steep-versus-shallow right is.

Efficiency comes from level curves of slope — ISOCLINES: the set where dy/dx = c. For dy/dx = x - y, slopes are 0 exactly on the line y = x, slopes are 1 on y = x - 1 — whole diagonals of parallel dashes at once. Spotting where slopes vanish (the nullcline) organizes the entire field in one stroke and answers 'where are the dashes horizontal?' instantly.

Dependence structure shapes the field's symmetry: if the DE involves ONLY x (dy/dx = 2x), every vertical line carries identical dashes — the field is column-uniform. Only y (dy/dx = y - 3): row-uniform. Both variables: the general case. This observation is the master key to the matching genre next.
key_terms: A dash of slope f(x, y) at each grid point — the DE drawn
Where the slope equals c / equals 0: whole curves of parallel dashes
x-only DEs repeat down columns; y-only DEs repeat across rows
boxes: ap_alert

When drawing field segments, three gradations are graded: horizontal where the slope is 0, 45-degree-ish where it is ±1, visibly steeper beyond. Dashes all drawn at the same tilt — the rushed student's field — loses the construction points wholesale.

sections.title: The Matching Genre
sections.subtitle: Which equation made this field?
sections.body:
Given a field and four candidate DEs, structural tests eliminate fast. Test 1 — uniformity: columns identical ⟹ the DE has no y; rows identical ⟹ no x. Test 2 — the zero set: find the horizontal dashes; their locations must satisfy RHS = 0 (horizontal along y = x? the equation vanishes there: consistent with dy/dx = x - y, not with dy/dx = x + y). Test 3 — a single point probe: evaluate each surviving candidate at one easy point with a distinctive dash and compare signs/steepness.

The three tests in that order settle nearly every matching question in under a minute, and each test is a one-line justification if the format demands work. Sign patterns by quadrant — 'slopes positive in quadrants I and III, negative in II and IV' suggests dy/dx = xy — extend test 3 across regions for the trickier sets.

The reverse genre — given the DE, pick the field — runs the same tests generatively: predict the uniformity, predict the nullcline, predict one quadrant's signs, then find the field exhibiting all three. Predict-then-match beats staring; the structure does the work.

Distractor fields are built by sign flips (the field of -f), variable swaps (the field of f(y, x)), and nullcline shifts. The three tests catch all three manufacturing methods — which is why they are the tests.
key_terms: Uniformity, zero set, point probe — in that order
Products like xy alternate signs by quadrant; sums change along lines
Generate the features from the DE, then find the field showing them
boxes: ap_alert

The nullcline test is the highest-yield single check: locate the horizontal dashes, set each candidate's right side to zero, and keep only candidates whose zero set passes through those dashes. One test typically eliminates three of four choices.

sections.title: Threading Solutions
sections.subtitle: Curves that follow the dashes
sections.body:
A solution curve through a point P threads the field: starting at P, it proceeds tangent to every dash it meets — the dashes are the curve's own tangent segments, prescribed in advance. Sketching one is a hand-eye exercise: from P, follow the local slope a short way, reassess, continue; backward from P the same. The result should never CROSS dashes at an angle — crossing means the sketch disobeyed the equation somewhere.

Quality criteria the readers apply: the curve passes through the required point; its slope at that point matches the local dash; it respects equilibria (never crossing a horizontal-dash line that represents an equilibrium solution — solutions cannot cross each other, in particular not the constant ones); and its end behavior follows the field's flow (flattening toward equilibria, steepening where dashes steepen).

The no-crossing principle has teeth: for dP/dt = P(10 - P), a solution starting at P = 3 stays trapped in the band 0 < P < 10 forever — the equilibria at 0 and 10 are walls. Threading respects the walls: the curve rises from 3, inflects, and flattens toward 10 without touching it. The trapped-between-equilibria reading answers limit questions ('lim t→∞ P = 10') without any formula.

Multiple threads from different anchors reveal the family: sketching solutions through three stacked points shows the family's structure — for x-only DEs the members are exact vertical translates of one another, and in general they are non-crossing curves filling the plane. The field plus threading IS the general solution, drawn instead of derived.
key_terms: Following the dashes tangentially from the anchor point, both directions
Solution curves never cross each other — equilibria are impassable walls
Between equilibria, solutions stay forever: limits read off the field
boxes: ap_alert

Sketched solutions are graded on three visible behaviors: through the point, tangent to the local dashes, and asymptotic to (never crossing) equilibrium lines. A sketch that touches the equilibrium loses the point — approach, don't arrive.

sections.title: Reading Without Solving
sections.subtitle: Qualitative analysis from the picture
sections.body:
Fields answer behavior questions formula-free. Where is the solution through (1, 2) increasing? Wherever the local slopes are positive along its path — read the dash signs. Where is it concave up? Where the dashes STEEPEN in the direction of travel (slopes increasing along the curve) — or, rigorously, differentiate the DE: for dy/dx = x - y, y'' = 1 - y' = 1 - (x - y), and the sign analysis runs on the formula. Field for intuition, implicit differentiation of the DE for certification.

The d²y/dx² computation deserves its own drill since BC asks it directly: differentiate the right side with respect to x, REMEMBERING y is a function of x (chain rule fees on every y). dy/dx = xy: y'' = y + xy' = y + x(xy) = y + x²y = y(1 + x²). Concavity of solutions now reads from y's sign alone — solutions above the x-axis are concave up everywhere. One differentiation, global conclusions.

Equilibrium stability reads from the flow: dashes pointing TOWARD an equilibrium line from both sides mark a stable (attracting) equilibrium — cooling toward room temperature; pointing away, unstable (repelling) — a pencil balanced on its tip. For the logistic field: P = 10 attracts (solutions converge), P = 0 repels (any positive start grows away). Stability vocabulary is not formally required by the AP, but the directional reading IS, phrased as limit questions.

The chapter's place in the arc: fields show every solution but name none. Euler's method (next) walks the field numerically when no formula exists; separation of variables (after) extracts formulas when the equation permits. Picture, number, formula — three resolutions of the same object, and the exam tests all three.
key_terms: Signs of slopes along the path: increasing/decreasing without solving
Differentiate the right side with chain-rule fees on y, then sign-analyze
Dashes converging on an equilibrium: attracting; diverging: repelling
boxes: ap_alert

'Find d²y/dx² in terms of x and y' is a BC standard: differentiate the DE's right side, substitute the DE itself for every dy/dx that appears, and present the result in x and y only. The substitute-the-DE-back step is the graded move.

mcq.explanation: Evaluate the right side: 3 - 1 = 2.

mcq.question: A slope field has identical dashes down every vertical line. The differential equation
mcq.explanation: Down a vertical line, x is fixed while y varies. Identical dashes there mean the slope ignores y entirely — the equation depends on x only.

mcq.explanation: Zero slope where the right side vanishes: y = 0 and y = 4 — the equilibrium lines.

mcq.question: A solution of dP/dt = P(6 - P) starts at P(0) = 2. Then lim t→∞ P(t) =
mcq.explanation: Between the equilibria 0 and 6 the rate is positive: P rises, trapped below the attracting wall at 6, approaching it.

mcq.question: For dy/dx = xy, the second derivative is y'' = y + x(xy) = y(1 + x²). Solutions BELOW the x-axis are
mcq.explanation: y(1 + x²) takes y's sign: negative y makes y'' < 0 at every x — concave down throughout.

frq.question:
Consider dy/dx = (x + 1)(y - 2).
(a) Compute the slopes at the six points (0,0), (1,0), (-1,0), (0,2), (2,2), (0,4), and describe the dash at each.
(b) Identify all lines along which the field's segments are horizontal.
(c) The solution through (0, 4): is it increasing or decreasing at that point, and can it ever reach y = 2? Justify.
rubric: (a) Slopes: -2, -4, 0, 0, 0, 2 respectively, with flat/steep descriptions
(b) Horizontal where (x+1)(y-2) = 0: the lines x = -1 and y = 2
(c) At (0,4): slope (1)(2) = 2 > 0, increasing
y = 2 is an equilibrium solution; other solutions cannot cross or reach it
frq.model_answer: (a) (0,0): (1)(-2) = -2, steep downhill. (1,0): (2)(-2) = -4, steeper downhill. (-1,0): 0, horizontal. (0,2): 0, horizontal. (2,2): 0, horizontal. (0,4): (1)(2) = 2, uphill. (b) Segments are horizontal where the product vanishes: along the vertical line x = -1 and along the horizontal line y = 2. (c) At (0, 4) the slope is +2: increasing. The constant function y = 2 is itself a solution (both sides vanish identically), and solution curves never cross one another — so the curve through (0, 4) stays above y = 2 forever, approaching it at most asymptotically (and here, moving away as x increases since slopes above the line with x > -1 are positive).

frq.question:
The differential equation dy/dx = x² - y has a slope field with dashes drawn on the grid [-2, 2] × [-2, 2].
(a) Along what curve are the dashes horizontal? (It is not a straight line.)
(b) Find d²y/dx² in terms of x and y, substituting the DE where needed.
(c) Use (b) to determine where solution curves have inflection points, and verify that the curve from (a) is NOT the inflection locus.
rubric: (a) Horizontal where y = x² — the parabola
(b) y'' = 2x - y' = 2x - (x² - y) = 2x - x² + y
(c) Inflections possible where y = x² - 2x
The two parabolas differ (x² vs x² - 2x): flat-slope locus ≠ inflection locus, verified
frq.model_answer: (a) Dashes are horizontal where x² - y = 0: along the parabola y = x². (b) Differentiate: y'' = 2x - dy/dx; substitute the DE: y'' = 2x - (x² - y) = 2x - x² + y. (c) Inflection candidates where y'' = 0: y = x² - 2x. This parabola is the inflection locus — and it is distinct from y = x² (they agree only at x = 0). The places where solutions are momentarily FLAT and the places where they change CONCAVITY are different curves: horizontal dashes mark extrema of solutions, not inflections, and the algebra confirms the geometric distinction.

frq.question:
A population follows dP/dt = 0.4P(1 - P/12), P in thousands.
(a) Find the equilibrium solutions and classify each as attracting or repelling using the sign of dP/dt on each side.
(b) A solution starts at P(0) = 3. Describe its long-term behavior and its monotonicity, with justification from the rate's sign.
(c) Using the DE, find the population at which dP/dt is maximized, and connect this to the inflection point of the solution curve.
rubric: (a) Equilibria P = 0, 12; rate negative below 0 region n/a, positive on (0,12), negative above 12: 0 repels, 12 attracts
(b) From 3: rate positive throughout (0,12): P increases monotonically toward 12; lim = 12
(c) Rate g(P) = 0.4P - P²/30 maximized at P = 6 (vertex/derivative)
P = 6 = L/2 is where P' peaks: the solution's inflection — fastest growth at half capacity
frq.model_answer: (a) dP/dt = 0 at P = 0 and P = 12. For 0 < P < 12 the rate is positive (both factors positive); for P > 12, negative. Solutions just above 0 move away from 0 (repelling); solutions on either side of 12 move toward it (attracting). (b) Starting at 3, the rate stays positive while P remains in (0, 12), so P increases for all time, trapped below the attracting equilibrium: monotonically increasing with lim t→∞ P = 12 thousand. (c) The rate as a function of P, g(P) = 0.4P(1 - P/12), is a downward parabola with roots 0 and 12: maximized at the midpoint P = 6. When P' is maximal, P'' changes sign — the solution curve inflects at P = 6 = L/2: the famous logistic property that growth is fastest at half the carrying capacity.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY: when no formula exists, walk. Euler's method takes the tangent-line step from Unit 4 and repeats it — step, re-aim, step again — turning any differential equation into arithmetic a spreadsheet could do. It is how computers actually solve DEs.
learning_objectives: Execute Euler's method: repeated tangent-line steps of size h
Organize the computation in the standard x, y, dy/dx, Δy table
Interpret Euler's method as following the slope field in straight chords
Determine over/underestimate direction from the solution's concavity
Understand step size's effect on accuracy and cost

sections.title: One Step, Then Another
sections.subtitle: The tangent line, iterated
sections.body:
Unit 4's tangent-line approximation took ONE step: y(x + h) ≈ y(x) + h·y'(x). Euler's method repeats it: from the new point, recompute the slope FROM THE DE, step again. Each step uses the equation's slope recipe at the current location — the method literally walks the slope field, replacing the curve with a chain of short chords.

The showcase, worked completely: dy/dx = x + y, y(0) = 1, step h = 0.5, approximate y(1). Step 1: slope at (0, 1) is 0 + 1 = 1; Δy = h·slope = 0.5; new point (0.5, 1.5). Step 2: slope at (0.5, 1.5) is 0.5 + 1.5 = 2; Δy = 1; new point (1, 2.5). Euler's approximation: y(1) ≈ 2.5. Two slope evaluations, two multiplications, two additions — arithmetic, organized.

The update rule in symbols: x_{new} = x_old + h; y_{new} = y_old + h·f(x_old, y_old). The slope is always evaluated at the OLD point — stepping with a slope from anywhere else is a different (and unasked) method. The AP's h is almost always 0.5 or 0.25 with two or three steps: small enough to test the iteration, large enough to keep arithmetic humane.

Why it works and when it doesn't: each chord follows the field exactly at its launch point and drifts as the true curve bends away. Smaller h means less drift per step (error per step shrinks like h²) but more steps; total error shrinks like h. Halving the step roughly halves the final error — the trade the last section quantifies.
key_terms: y_{new} = y_old + h·f(x_old, y_old): tangent steps, slope re-evaluated each time
Each step launches with the field's slope at its starting point
Chords leave the bending curve; error per step ~h², total ~h
boxes: ap_alert

Euler questions on the BC exam are two or three steps by design — enough to force the re-evaluation of the slope at each new point. Using the ORIGINAL point's slope for every step (the one-tangent-line error) is the planted mistake; the slope must be recomputed from the DE each step.

sections.title: The Table Discipline
sections.subtitle: Four columns that prevent disasters
sections.body:
The standard table has four columns: x, y, dy/dx (evaluated from the DE at the current x and y), and Δy = h·(dy/dx). Each row's x and y feed the slope; the slope feeds Δy; Δy plus the current y becomes the NEXT row's y. The chain structure means one arithmetic slip corrupts everything after — the table's visibility is what lets you (and the grader) audit each link.

The showcase in table form: row 1: x = 0, y = 1, y' = 1, Δy = 0.5. Row 2: x = 0.5, y = 1.5, y' = 2, Δy = 1. Row 3: x = 1, y = 2.5 — the answer, with every intermediate value displayed. FRQ scoring typically awards the method (table structure with correct slope evaluations) and the answer separately; a transcription slip with a correct table loses one point, not both.

Variable bookkeeping for non-(x, y) equations: dT/dt = -0.3(T - 20) tables as t, T, dT/dt, ΔT — same discipline, renamed columns. Mixed-variable slopes (f depends on both) demand BOTH coordinates at evaluation time; t-only or y-only equations simplify the slope column but not the structure.

Calculator-section Euler problems allow arithmetic by machine, but the table must still appear — 'answer 2.5' floating alone earns the answer point at most. No-calculator Euler keeps numbers tame (halves and quarters); messy decimals in your table usually signal an evaluation error upstream, which is itself useful feedback mid-exam.
key_terms: x, y, dy/dx (from the DE), Δy = h·slope — the auditable layout
Each row feeds the next; visible intermediate values localize errors
Method points for the table, answer point for the final value
boxes: ap_alert

Write the table even when the calculator does the arithmetic — Euler FRQs award the setup. The four-column format with the DE-evaluated slope visible in each row IS the rubric's method point; mental math leaves it uncollected.

sections.title: Over or Under, Part 3
sections.subtitle: Concavity calls it, again
sections.body:
Euler chords are tangent-line segments, so the linearization error analysis transfers wholesale: if the true solution is CONCAVE UP on the interval, every chord sits below the curve and Euler UNDERestimates; concave down, overestimates. One geometric principle, third appearance (linearization, trapezoids' mirror, now Euler) — the exam asks it with each tool and accepts the same one-sentence justification shape.

Certifying concavity uses the previous chapter's move: compute y'' by differentiating the DE and substituting it back. For dy/dx = x + y: y'' = 1 + y' = 1 + x + y, positive along our path (every value is positive) — concave up, so 2.5 underestimates the true y(1). The exact solution (verifiable by substitution) is y = 2eˣ - x - 1, giving y(1) = 2e - 2 ≈ 3.44; indeed 2.5 < 3.44 ✓ — and notice how LARGE the gap is at h = 0.5: Euler is honest but crude at coarse steps.

The justification sentence, graded: 'y'' = 1 + x + y > 0 along the interval, so the solution is concave up; Euler's tangent segments lie below the curve, making the approximation an underestimate.' Compute y'', sign it on the relevant region, conclude with the geometry. Three beats, as ever.

The caveat that keeps it honest: the verdict needs single-signed concavity over the whole stepped interval. A solution inflecting mid-walk mixes the chord errors, and 'cannot be determined from concavity alone' becomes the correct answer — a choice the exam includes precisely for that case.
key_terms: Concave up ⟹ Euler under; concave down ⟹ over — linearization's law, iterated
Differentiate the DE, substitute it back, sign the result on the path
An inflection mid-walk voids the simple verdict
boxes: ap_alert

Euler over/under questions are the SAME rubric as linearization's: y'' computed from the DE, its sign on the interval, the chord-position conclusion. Students who connect the three appearances (tangent line, trapezoid, Euler) write this justification on autopilot.

sections.title: Step Size and the Method's Place
sections.subtitle: Accuracy, cost, and what Euler really is
sections.body:
Halving h doubles the steps and roughly halves the total error — first-order convergence. The showcase with h = 0.25 (four steps): y-values 1 → 1.25 → 1.625 → 2.156 → 2.852, against ≈3.44 exact: better than 2.5, still under (concave up), still crude. Euler's virtue is not precision; it is UNIVERSALITY — any first-order DE, any starting point, arithmetic only.

The exam tests the trade conceptually: 'how would the approximation change with a smaller step?' — closer to the true value, from the same side (concavity unchanged), at the cost of more steps. Production solvers use refined descendants (midpoint/RK4 evaluate trial slopes mid-step), but their souls are Euler's: step, re-aim, step. The AP requires only Euler, plus this awareness that it is the seed of the real thing.

Euler complements the unit's other resolutions: the slope field SHOWS all solutions, Euler NUMBERS one of them, separation (next) NAMES the nameable ones. FRQs braid them: sketch on the field, Euler two steps, then solve exactly and compare — the same IVP through three instruments. The braid rewards knowing what each instrument can and cannot say: fields give behavior, Euler gives a number with a known bias, formulas give everything but exist rarely.

A closing connection BC students should carry: Euler's method IS the tangent-line approximation composed with itself, which makes it the discrete shadow of the integral — summing slope×step is a Riemann sum of dy/dx. The method's error analysis, its refinement into better solvers, and its kinship with numerical integration are one subject; the AP shows you its doorway.
key_terms: Total error ~h: halve the step, halve the error, double the work
Any first-order DE, arithmetic only — the method's actual virtue
Field (behavior), Euler (number), separation (formula) — braided on FRQs
boxes: ap_alert

'With a smaller step size, the Euler approximation would be ___' — closer to the true value AND on the same side of it (the concavity hasn't changed). Both halves of that answer are expected when the question asks for the effect of refining h.

choices.D: changes which side of the true value the estimate falls on

mcq.explanation: First-order method: error ~h. The estimate's side is set by concavity, not by h.

frq.question:
Consider dy/dx = x - 2y with y(0) = 2.
(a) Use Euler's method with two steps of h = 0.5 to approximate y(1), presenting the four-column table.
(b) Compute d²y/dx² in terms of x and y, and evaluate the solution's concavity near the starting point.
(c) Based on (b), is your Euler answer an over- or underestimate? Justify.
rubric: (c) Concave up along the early path ⟹ chords below the curve ⟹ underestimate
Caveat or check that concavity stays positive on the walked region (it does along the computed path)
frq.model_answer: (a) Table — x | y | dy/dx | Δy: row 1: 0 | 2 | 0 - 4 = -4 | -2. Row 2: 0.5 | 0 | 0.5 - 0 = 0.5 | 0.25. Final: x = 1, y ≈ 0.25. (b) Differentiate: y'' = 1 - 2y'; substitute the DE: y'' = 1 - 2(x - 2y) = 1 - 2x + 4y. At (0, 2): y'' = 9 > 0, and along the computed path (y ≥ 0, x ≤ 1) it stays positive. (c) With the solution concave up on the stepped interval, Euler's tangent-line chords lie below the curve, so y(1) ≈ 0.25 is an UNDERestimate of the true value.

frq.question:
The temperature of an engine part obeys dT/dt = -0.4(T - 30), T(0) = 110, t in minutes.
(a) Approximate T(1) using Euler's method with h = 0.5.
(b) The exact solution is T(t) = 30 + 80e^{-0.4t}. Compute T(1) exactly (in terms of e) and numerically, and find the Euler error.
(c) Explain the error's direction using the solution's concavity, computed from the DE.
rubric: (b) Exact: 30 + 80e^{-0.4} ≈ 83.62; error ≈ -2.42 (Euler low)
(c) T'' = -0.4T' = 0.16(T - 30) > 0 while T > 30: concave up
Chords below a concave-up curve: Euler underestimates — matching the computed error
frq.model_answer: (a) Step 1: slope = -0.4(110 - 30) = -32; ΔT = -16; T(0.5) ≈ 94. Step 2: slope = -0.4(64) = -25.6; ΔT = -12.8; T(1) ≈ 81.2°. (b) Exact: T(1) = 30 + 80e^{-0.4} ≈ 30 + 53.62 = 83.62°. Euler's error: 81.2 - 83.62 ≈ -2.4° — the method ran low. (c) T'' = -0.4·dT/dt = -0.4·(-0.4(T - 30)) = 0.16(T - 30), positive while T > 30: the cooling curve is concave up (steep drop flattening out). Euler's chords therefore undershoot the curve, exactly the negative error observed.

frq.question:
For the IVP dy/dx = y - x with y(0) = 0.5:
(a) Run Euler's method with h = 0.25 for two steps to approximate y(0.5).
(b) A classmate runs the same problem with h = 0.5 (one step) and gets y(0.5) ≈ 0.75. Compare the two approximations and state which should be more accurate, with the general principle.
(c) Verify that y = x + 1 - 0.5eˣ solves the IVP, and compute the true y(0.5) to assess both approximations.
rubric: (b) Smaller h ⟹ less drift: the h = 0.25 run should be closer (same side)
True y(0.5) = 1.5 - 0.5e^{0.5} ≈ 0.6756; indeed 0.7188 vs 0.75: smaller h closer, both over
frq.model_answer: (a) Step 1: slope at (0, 0.5) = 0.5 - 0 = 0.5; Δy = 0.125; → (0.25, 0.625). Step 2: slope = 0.625 - 0.25 = 0.375; Δy ≈ 0.09375; → y(0.5) ≈ 0.71875. (b) The h = 0.25 estimate should beat the h = 0.5 one: Euler's total error scales roughly with h, so halving the step halves the drift. Both lie on the same side of the truth (set by concavity, not step size). (c) For y = x + 1 - 0.5eˣ: y' = 1 - 0.5eˣ, and y - x = 1 - 0.5eˣ — equal ✓; y(0) = 0 + 1 - 0.5 = 0.5 ✓. True value: y(0.5) = 1.5 - 0.5e^{0.5} ≈ 0.6756. The approximations 0.71875 (h = 0.25) and 0.75 (h = 0.5) are both high — y'' = y' - 1 = -0.5eˣ < 0, concave down, so Euler overestimates — and the smaller step is closer, as predicted.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: When a differential equation lets you herd every y to one side and every x to the other, two integrals finish the job. Separation of variables is the unit's formula machine — and the source of the exponential solutions every science class asserts.
learning_objectives: Identify separable equations: dy/dx expressible as g(x)·h(y)
Execute the separation ritual: separate, integrate both sides, solve for y
Apply initial conditions at the optimal stage and resolve the constant
Convert C-bearing exponential forms via the ±e^C → A consolidation
Track domains and lost solutions through the separation process

sections.title: Separate, Integrate, Solve
sections.subtitle: The ritual on a first example
sections.body:
A DE is SEPARABLE when the right side factors into (function of x)·(function of y): dy/dx = g(x)h(y). The ritual: (1) SEPARATE — move all y's left with dy, all x's right with dx: dy/h(y) = g(x) dx (the Leibniz differentials, manipulated as Unit 4 licensed); (2) INTEGRATE both sides, one +C on the right; (3) SOLVE for y if asked, applying the initial condition at the cleanest moment.

Worked: dy/dx = xy², y(0) = 1. Separate: y^{-2} dy = x dx. Integrate: -y^{-1} = x²/2 + C. Apply the condition NOW (before solving for y): -1 = 0 + C, so C = -1. Solve: -1/y = x²/2 - 1, hence y = 1/(1 - x²/2) = 2/(2 - x²). Verify by differentiating if time permits; the check is one chain rule.

Not everything separates: dy/dx = x + y has an inseparable sum (no factoring rescues it — that one needs other methods and appears on the AP only via fields and Euler). The separability CHECK is a factoring question: can the right side be written as a pure-x factor times a pure-y factor? Sums of x-stuff and y-stuff: no. Products and quotients: usually yes.

The one-constant convention: both integrals generate constants, but their difference is a single constant — write +C on one side only, immediately. Two C's that later merge are harmless but waste motion; the convention is standard and graders expect it.
key_terms: dy/dx = g(x)h(y): the right side factors by variable
Separate (dy with y's, dx with x's), integrate both sides, solve for y
Pin C right after integrating — before the algebra of solving for y
boxes: ap_alert

Separation FRQs allocate points for: the separated form (visible!), both antiderivatives, the constant's resolution, and the final explicit solution. Skipping the visible separation step — integrating 'in your head' — forfeits the first point even with everything else right.

sections.title: The Exponential Family, Derived
sections.subtitle: Where Ce^{kt} actually comes from
sections.body:
The unit's flagship: dy/dt = ky. Separate: dy/y = k dt. Integrate: ln|y| = kt + C. Exponentiate: |y| = e^{kt + C} = e^C·e^{kt}, so y = ±e^C e^{kt} — and the cluster ±e^C, an arbitrary nonzero constant, consolidates to A: y = Ae^{kt}. (A = 0 quietly readmits the equilibrium y = 0 lost when we divided by y; the final family is complete.)

That consolidation — ±e^C becomes A — is the chapter's most-tested algebra. e^C is positive; the ± restores both signs; naming the cluster A is both legal and expected. Exam answers left as y = e^{kt + C} are unfinished; answers asserting A = e^C (dropping the ±) are subtly wrong when the initial condition is negative. The clean line: 'let A = ±e^C, so y = Ae^{kt}; then A = y(0).'

With an initial condition the whole derivation compresses: y(0) = y₀ gives A = y₀ directly, and y = y₀e^{kt}. Doubling times and half-lives now COMPUTE instead of being quoted: half-life solves y₀e^{kT} = y₀/2, so T = ln(½)/k = ln2/|k| for decay. The science-class facts are this separation, finished.

Newton's cooling separates identically with a shift: dT/(T - T_env) = -k dt gives ln|T - T_env| = -kt + C, so T = T_env + Ae^{-kt} — exponential decay OF THE GAP. One substitution (u = T - T_env) reduces cooling to the flagship; recognizing shifted exponentials is half the unit's modeling fluency.
key_terms: y' = ky separates to ln|y| = kt + C, consolidating to y = Ae^{kt}
The consolidation that absorbs sign and constant — with A = 0 readmitting the equilibrium
Cooling: the GAP T - T_env decays exponentially; T = T_env + Ae^{-kt}
boxes: ap_alert

After exponentiating ln|y| = kt + C, the graded sequence is: |y| = e^C e^{kt}, then y = Ae^{kt} with A = ±e^C. Jumping straight from the log line to y = Ce^{kt} is usually tolerated WITH the absolute value handled — but writing it out once protects the point and your sign when y₀ < 0.

sections.title: Implicit Solutions and Lost Members
sections.subtitle: When y won't isolate, and who fell in the division
sections.body:
Some separations end implicitly: dy/dx = x/y separates to y dy = x dx, integrating to y²/2 = x²/2 + C, i.e., y² - x² = K — hyperbolas, perfectly good solution curves with no global y = formula. The AP accepts implicit answers when isolating y is impossible or ugly, PROVIDED the constant is resolved: with y(1) = 2, K = 3, and the solution is the branch of y² = x² + 3 through (1, 2): y = +√(x² + 3) (the sign chosen by the initial point).

The branch selection is graded: y² = x² + 3 alone names two curves; the initial condition's sign picks y = +√(x² + 3), and SAYING so — 'taking the positive root since y(1) = 2 > 0' — is the expected sentence. Implicit-to-explicit conversion, when demanded, is exactly this: solve, then choose by the anchor.

Division's casualties: separating dy/h(y) divided by h(y), quietly assuming h(y) ≠ 0 — and each root of h is a constant solution potentially LOST. For dy/dx = y(y - 3): dividing by y(y - 3) loses y = 0 and y = 3, the equilibria. Complete answers acknowledge them; IVPs anchored AT an equilibrium (y(0) = 3) are answered by the constant solution alone, no separation needed — a shortcut the exam plants.

Domain honesty from chapter 1 returns at the finish: y = 2/(2 - x²) through (0, 1) lives on (-√2, √2) — the interval around the anchor where the denominator survives. Solving FRQs end with the explicit function; the strongest answers append its valid interval when blow-ups lurk.
key_terms: An x-y relation with C resolved — acceptable when y won't isolate
The initial condition's sign chooses the root: state the choice
Dividing by h(y) discards h's roots — recover them or anchor on them directly
boxes: ap_alert

If the initial condition sits AT an equilibrium (y(0) = 3 for dy/dx = y(y-3)), the answer is the constant function y = 3 — separation is unnecessary and dividing by zero to attempt it is wrong. Check the anchor against the equilibria before separating; it is a two-second scan.

sections.title: The Genre at Full Strength
sections.subtitle: A complete FRQ anatomy
sections.body:
The classic separation FRQ braids the unit: given dy/dx = (6x²)/(2y) with y(1) = 4 — (a) slope field dashes at marked points (chapter 2 mechanics); (b) Euler or tangent-line estimate of y(1.1) (chapter 3 / Unit 4); (c) solve exactly. The solve: 2y dy = 6x² dx; y² = 2x³ + C; 16 = 2 + C so C = 14; y = +√(2x³ + 14), positive root by y(1) = 4 > 0. Three instruments, one equation — the braid in its natural habitat.

Part (c)'s rubric, typical of the genre: one point for separation, one for both antiderivatives, one for resolving C (with the condition applied to the IMPLICIT form — fine and encouraged), one for the explicit solution with the correct branch. Four points, four visible moves. The moves are this chapter's sections in order.

Time-of-event finales decorate the genre: 'find when y = 6' solves 36 = 2x³ + 14, x³ = 11, x = 11^{1/3}. The solved formula converts behavior questions into algebra — which is the whole point of having a formula, and why the exam asks one such finale routinely.

The unit's last two chapters apply the machine: exponential models (population, decay, cooling — chapter 5) and the logistic equation (chapter 6), whose separation runs through partial fractions and rewards everything Unit 6 built. The ritual is learned; what remains is running it on the models that matter.
key_terms: Field + Euler + exact solve on one IVP — the unit's standard assembly
Separation, antiderivatives, constant, explicit branch — each visible
Solved formulas turn 'when does y reach 6?' into algebra
boxes: ap_alert

Apply the initial condition to the IMPLICIT line (y² = 2x³ + C) rather than after isolating y — fewer symbols, no premature branch choice, same credit. Then isolate, choosing the branch by the condition's sign. This ordering is both faster and safer.

mcq.explanation: The flagship separation: ln|y| = -3t + C consolidates to y = Ae^{-3t}.

mcq.explanation: y² = x² + C with 4 = 1 + C: C = 3. The initial y is negative: take the negative root.
