mcq.explanation: The anchor sits ON the equilibrium y = 5 (the rate vanishes there): the constant solution is the answer, no separation required.

frq.question:
Consider dy/dx = (3x²)/(2y) with y(0) = 2.
(a) Solve the differential equation, applying the initial condition at the implicit stage.
(b) State the explicit solution with the correct branch, and give its domain.
(c) Find the value of x at which y = 4.
rubric: (a) 2y dy = 3x² dx → y² = x³ + C; 4 = 0 + C: y² = x³ + 4
(b) y = +√(x³ + 4) (positive branch since y(0) = 2 > 0); domain x³ > -4: x > -4^{1/3}
Branch-selection sentence present
frq.model_answer: (a) Separate: 2y dy = 3x² dx. Integrate: y² = x³ + C. Apply y(0) = 2 now: 4 = C. Implicit solution: y² = x³ + 4. (b) Since y(0) = 2 > 0, take the positive root: y = √(x³ + 4), valid where x³ + 4 > 0, i.e., on (-∛4, ∞) — the interval containing the anchor x = 0. (c) y = 4: 16 = x³ + 4, x³ = 12, x = ∛12 ≈ 2.289.

frq.question:
A radioactive sample obeys dm/dt = km (k < 0), with m(0) = 80 grams and m(10) = 40 grams (t in years).
(a) Derive the general solution by separation, showing the ±e^C consolidation.
(b) Use the two data points to find A and k exactly.
(c) Find the time at which 10 grams remain.
rubric: (a) dm/m = k dt → ln|m| = kt + C → m = Ae^{kt}, A = ±e^C
Exact-form k and the three-half-lives logic (or algebra) for (c)
frq.model_answer: (a) Separate: dm/m = k dt. Integrate: ln|m| = kt + C. Exponentiate: |m| = e^C e^{kt}, so m = Ae^{kt} where A = ±e^C (and A = 0 would readmit the trivial equilibrium). (b) m(0) = A = 80. Then 40 = 80e^{10k} gives e^{10k} = 1/2, k = -ln 2/10 per year. (c) 10 = 80e^{kt}: e^{kt} = 1/8 = (1/2)³, so kt = 3 ln(1/2), t = 3·ln(1/2)/(ln(1/2)/10) = 30 years — three half-lives, as 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 confirms.

frq.question:
Consider the equation dy/dx = (y - 1)cos x.
(a) Find all equilibrium solutions.
(b) Solve the IVP with y(0) = 3, showing the consolidation of constants.
(c) Show that the solution from (b) never crosses the equilibrium, by examining the solution formula.
rubric: (a) Equilibrium: y = 1
(b) dy/(y-1) = cos x dx → ln|y-1| = sin x + C → y = 1 + Ae^{sin x}; A = 2: y = 1 + 2e^{sin x}
(c) 2e^{sin x} > 0 always: y > 1 for all x
Connects to the no-crossing principle: the formula certifies what the field predicted
frq.model_answer: (a) The rate vanishes identically when y = 1: the single equilibrium solution. (b) Separate: dy/(y - 1) = cos x dx. Integrate: ln|y - 1| = sin x + C. Exponentiate and consolidate: |y - 1| = e^C e^{sin x}, so y - 1 = Ae^{sin x} with A = ±e^C. The condition: 3 - 1 = Ae⁰, A = 2. Solution: y = 1 + 2e^{sin x}. (c) The term 2e^{sin x} is positive for every x (exponentials never vanish), so y stays strictly above 1 forever — bounded between 1 + 2e^{-1} and 1 + 2e by the sine's range, oscillating but never touching the equilibrium. The formula certifies the no-crossing principle the slope field promised.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Compound interest, carbon dating, viral spread before saturation — one equation governs them all: dy/dt = ky. You derived its solution last chapter; now you'll run the model end to end, from data to constants to predictions.
learning_objectives: Recognize 'rate proportional to amount' contexts as dy/dt = ky models
Use y = y₀e^{kt} with data points to determine k exactly
Compute half-lives and doubling times, and convert between them and k
Solve dating, finance, and population problems through the model
Distinguish exponential from other growth patterns in data and language

sections.title: The Model and Its Fingerprint
sections.subtitle: Constant relative rate
sections.body:
dy/dt = ky says the rate of change is proportional to the current amount — equivalently, the RELATIVE rate y'/y is the constant k. Per-capita birth rates, per-dollar interest, per-atom decay probability: whenever each unit of the quantity contributes equally to its own change, the model applies and the solution is y = y₀e^{kt} (last chapter's flagship separation, with y₀ the starting amount).

The fingerprint in data: equal time steps multiply the amount by equal FACTORS. A population hitting 100, 150, 225, 337.5 at consecutive hours is exponential (×1.5 each step); one hitting 100, 150, 200, 250 is linear (+50 each step). The exam tests the distinction in both directions — recognize the pattern, or produce values matching a named pattern.

The sign of k narrates: k > 0 grows, k < 0 decays, and |k| sets the speed. Units of k are 'per time' (per year, per hour) — y'/y has the amount's units canceling. An interest rate of 5% per year compounding continuously IS k = 0.05 per year; the finance phrasing and the calculus phrasing are the same statement.

What the model ignores — and where it breaks: nothing limits growth (no carrying capacity), nothing exhausts decay (the amount never reaches zero). Real systems obey it only in regimes far from limits: early epidemics, small populations, the first half-lives. The logistic model next chapter installs the ceiling; knowing WHICH model a stem describes is itself a graded reading skill.
key_terms: dy/dt = ky ⟺ y = y₀e^{kt}: constant relative rate y'/y = k
Equal time steps multiply by equal factors — the data signature
No limits in the model: it fits growth far from ceilings, decay far from zero
boxes: ap_alert

'Grows at a rate proportional to its size' ⟹ exponential. 'Grows at a CONSTANT rate' ⟹ linear (dy/dt = c). The two phrases sit one word apart and name different universes — the exam exploits the near-collision regularly.

sections.title: Finding k from Data
sections.subtitle: Two points determine the model
sections.body:
With y₀ known, one more data point pins k. A culture starts at 500 bacteria and reaches 1500 after 4 hours: 1500 = 500e^{4k}, so e^{4k} = 3 and k = (ln 3)/4 per hour. Keep k EXACT — (ln 3)/4, not 0.2747 — because later parts reuse it and rounding propagates. The exact-k habit is worth real points across multi-part FRQs.

When y₀ is unknown too, two data points make two equations; dividing them cancels y₀: y(7)/y(3) = e^{7k}/e^{3k} = e^{4k}. The RATIO of values across a time gap depends only on k and the gap — a structural fact that solves 'the population triples every 5 hours' instantly: e^{5k} = 3 regardless of the start.

Predictions then evaluate the finished formula: with k = (ln 3)/4 and y₀ = 500, the population at t = 10 is 500e^{10(ln3)/4} = 500·3^{2.5} ≈ 7794. Note the clean form 3^{10/4}: exponentials with exact k often simplify through the base the data suggested — writing e^{kt} as (e^{4k})^{t/4} = 3^{t/4} both checks the work and speeds evaluation.

Inverse questions solve for t: when does the culture reach 10,000? 10000 = 500·3^{t/4}, so 3^{t/4} = 20 and t = 4·ln 20/ln 3 ≈ 10.9 hours. Take logs, isolate t — the algebra is one move once the formula stands.
key_terms: k = (ln 3)/4, never its decimal — later parts reuse it
y(t₂)/y(t₁) = e^{k(t₂-t₁)}: ratios see only k and the gap, not y₀
e^{kt} = 3^{t/4} when e^{4k} = 3 — the data's own base simplifies everything
boxes: ap_alert

Solve for k symbolically BEFORE any decimals: 'e^{4k} = 3, so k = (ln 3)/4.' FRQ rubrics award the exact expression, and decimal-first work loses both precision and the simplification 3^{t/4} that makes part (c) humane.

sections.title: Half-Life and Doubling Time
sections.subtitle: The model's natural clocks
sections.body:
The half-life T_{1/2} of a decaying quantity solves y₀e^{kT} = y₀/2: T_{1/2} = ln(1/2)/k = (ln 2)/|k|. It is INDEPENDENT of the starting amount — every half-life halves whatever is present, which is why 'three half-lives' means ×1/8 regardless of scale. Doubling time mirrors for growth: T_double = (ln 2)/k.

The conversion runs both ways: carbon-14's half-life of 5730 years gives k = -ln 2/5730 per year; an investment doubling every 9 years has k = ln 2/9 ≈ 0.077 — the 'rule of 72' from finance (72 divided by the percentage rate estimates the doubling years) is this formula's folklore approximation — ln 2 ≈ 0.693 suggests 69.3, but 72 has friendlier divisors. The calculus version is exact.

Dating problems run the clock backward: a sample retains 30% of its carbon-14 — how old? 0.30 = e^{kt} with k = -ln2/5730: t = ln(0.30)/k = 5730·ln(0.30)/ln(0.5) ≈ 9953 years. The structure: measured fraction = e^{kt}, logs, solve. Whole-number half-life counts need no logs at all (1/8 remaining = 3 half-lives = 17,190 years); fractional ones do.

A notational fork to read carefully: some texts write decay as y = y₀e^{-λt} with λ > 0. Then the half-life is (ln 2)/λ — same mathematics, the sign housed in the symbol instead of the constant. The exam declares its convention in the stem; mirror whichever it uses.
key_terms: T = (ln 2)/k for growth — the mirror clock
Measured fraction = e^{kt}; logs isolate the age
boxes: ap_alert

Half-life is independent of the amount — '800 g has the same half-life as 80 g' — and the exam tests the fact directly as a conceptual MC. Any answer choice making the half-life depend on y₀ is self-eliminating.

sections.title: The Model in Full Dress
sections.subtitle: A complete FRQ walkthrough
sections.body:
Anatomy of the standard exponential FRQ: 'A tank's pollutant decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. Initially 200 g; after 3 hours, 120 g.' (a) Write the DE: dy/dt = ky (the sentence IS the equation — translation point). (b) Solve it: y = 200e^{kt} (separation or citation of the known family — both accepted when the family is derived elsewhere on the exam). (c) Find k: 120 = 200e^{3k}, k = (1/3)ln(3/5). (d) Predict: y(10) = 200e^{10k} = 200(3/5)^{10/3} ≈ 36.5 g. (e) When does 10 g remain? t = ln(0.05)/k ≈ 17.6 hours.

Each part's graded element: the DE from the words; the family with the constant resolved; exact k; a prediction with units; an inverse solve. Five beats — and every exponential FRQ for a decade has been some subset of them, reordered and recostumed.

The with-inflow variant raises difficulty one notch: dy/dt = ky + r (decay plus constant replenishment) is NOT pure exponential, but it separates: dy/(ky + r) = dt, yielding shifted exponentials approaching the equilibrium y = -r/k. The cooling equation was exactly this shape. Recognizing 'proportional plus constant' as a separable shifted-exponential is the unit's second-tier skill, tested on harder FRQs.

Language rigor at the finish: 'the amount approaches zero but never reaches it' — exponential decay's tail is asymptotic, and claims of arrival ('the pollutant is gone at t = 50') are model-false. When asked for long-run behavior: lim t→∞ y = 0 (pure decay) or the equilibrium (with inflow), stated as a limit. The model speaks in asymptotes; answers should too.
key_terms: DE from words, solve, exact k, prediction with units, inverse solve
dy/dt = ky + r: separable, shifted exponential, equilibrium -r/k
Exponentials approach limits and never arrive — answer with limits
boxes: ap_alert

When the model adds a constant term (leak plus inflow, decay plus dosing), do NOT force y = y₀e^{kt} onto it — separate dy/(ky + r) = dt honestly. The pure-exponential reflex applied to mixed models is the second-tier FRQ's designed failure mode.

mcq.question: A population grows at a rate proportional to its size, starting at 800 with k = 0.02 per year. The model is
mcq.explanation: dy/dt = ky with y₀ = 800 solves to y₀e^{kt}. (D is discrete annual compounding — close numerically, not the continuous model.)

mcq.question: A sample decays from 500 g to 100 g in 8 days. The exact decay constant k is
mcq.explanation: 100 = 500e^{8k} gives e^{8k} = 1/5, so k = (1/8)ln(1/5) — negative, as decay demands.

mcq.question: A substance has half-life 20 years. Starting from 240 g, the amount after 60 years is
mcq.explanation: 60 years is three half-lives: 240 → 120 → 60 → 30.

mcq.question: An account doubles every 12 years under continuous growth. Its rate constant k is
mcq.explanation: e^{12k} = 2 ⟹ k = (ln 2)/12 per year.

mcq.question: Data: a quantity reads 64, 48, 36, 27 at equal time intervals. The pattern is

choices.A: exponential decay — each step multiplies by 3/4

mcq.explanation: Ratios: 48/64 = 36/48 = 27/36 = 3/4 — equal factors, the exponential fingerprint. (The differences -16, -12, -9 are unequal, killing linear.)

frq.question:
The pollutant in a pond decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. At t = 0 there are 200 grams; at t = 3 hours, 120 grams remain.
(a) Write and solve the differential equation, giving y(t) with exact constants.
(b) Find the half-life of the pollutant, exactly and to the nearest tenth of an hour.
(c) Determine, with a limit statement, the long-run amount — and explain why the model never reports exactly zero grams.
rubric: (c) lim t→∞ y = 0
Exponentials are positive for all finite t: asymptotic approach, never arrival
frq.model_answer: (a) The sentence translates to dy/dt = ky. Separating (or citing the family): y = 200e^{kt}. Fitting: 120 = 200e^{3k}, e^{3k} = 3/5, k = (1/3)ln(3/5) per hour (negative ✓). (b) Half-life: e^{kT} = 1/2 ⟹ T = ln(1/2)/k = 3·ln(1/2)/ln(3/5) ≈ 4.1 hours. (c) lim t→∞ 200e^{kt} = 0 since k < 0. But e^{kt} > 0 for every finite t — the model halves and halves without ever producing zero: decay is asymptotic, and 'the pollutant is gone at time T' is a statement the model cannot make.

frq.question:
Archaeologists find a wooden tool retaining 22% of its original carbon-14. Carbon-14's half-life is 5730 years.
(a) Find the decay constant k exactly.
(b) Determine the tool's age to the nearest century.
(c) The lab's measurement could be off by ±2 percentage points (so the true fraction lies in [0.20, 0.24]). Compute the corresponding age range and comment on the sensitivity.
rubric: Comment: ±2 points of fraction ⟹ roughly ∓750 years — logs compress, but old samples stay sensitive
frq.model_answer: (a) e^{5730k} = 1/2 gives k = -ln 2/5730 per year. (b) 0.22 = e^{kt}: t = ln(0.22)/k = 5730·ln(0.22)/ln(0.5) ≈ 12,517 — about 12,500 years old. (c) At 0.20: t = 5730·ln(0.20)/ln(0.5) ≈ 13,305. At 0.24: ≈ 11,799. The age range is roughly 11,800–13,300 years: a ±2-point measurement uncertainty swings the date by about ±750 years. The logarithm softens the sensitivity (fractions enter through ln), but for ancient, low-fraction samples each percentage point still moves centuries — why labs report dating with explicit error bars.

frq.question:
A hospital patient receives medication by continuous IV drip at 12 mg per hour, while the body eliminates the drug at a rate proportional to the amount present, with constant 0.3 per hour. Let y(t) be the milligrams in the bloodstream, y(0) = 0.
(a) Write the differential equation for y.
(b) Find the equilibrium level and interpret it.
(c) Solve the equation by separation and find how long until the level reaches half the equilibrium value.
rubric: (b) Equilibrium: 12 - 0.3y = 0 → y = 40 mg — inflow balances elimination
Shifted-exponential structure handled (not forced into pure y₀e^{kt})
frq.model_answer: (a) Rate in minus rate out: dy/dt = 12 - 0.3y. (b) Setting the rate to zero: y = 40 mg — the steady state where the drip's 12 mg/h exactly matches the body's elimination 0.3(40) = 12 mg/h. The level approaches 40 and stabilizes there. (c) Separate: dy/(12 - 0.3y) = dt; integrating, -(1/0.3)ln|12 - 0.3y| = t + C. With y(0) = 0: C = -(1/0.3)ln 12. Solving: 12 - 0.3y = 12e^{-0.3t}, so y = 40(1 - e^{-0.3t}). Half the equilibrium: 20 = 40(1 - e^{-0.3t}) gives e^{-0.3t} = 1/2, t = ln 2/0.3 ≈ 2.31 hours — the system's own 'half-life' clock, now measuring approach instead of decay.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY, and the unit's crown jewel: real populations can't grow forever. The logistic equation installs a ceiling, bends the exponential into an S-curve, and hands the BC exam its favorite collection of no-solving-required questions.
learning_objectives: Interpret the logistic equation dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L) and its carrying capacity L
Determine limits, equilibria, and behavior from the equation without solving
Locate the inflection at P = L/2 where growth is fastest
Use the solution form P = L/(1 + Ae^{-kt}) with initial conditions
Answer the AP's standard logistic battery: limits, fastest growth, concavity

sections.title: Installing the Ceiling
sections.subtitle: Reading the logistic equation
sections.body:
dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L): growth proportional to the population AND to the remaining fraction of capacity. When P is small, (1 - P/L) ≈ 1 and the equation is nearly exponential — unchecked early growth. As P nears L, the factor collapses toward zero and growth chokes. The constant L — the CARRYING CAPACITY — is the environment's ceiling, and k sets the intrinsic speed.

Equilibria from the algebra: dP/dt = 0 at P = 0 and P = L. Signs between: for 0 < P < L both factors are positive — populations grow; for P > L the second factor is negative — overcrowded populations shrink back. So L attracts from both sides and 0 repels: every positive start converges to L. The limit statement lim t→∞ P(t) = L (for P₀ > 0) is the single most-asked logistic fact, and it reads straight off the equation.

Alternative costumes the exam wears: dP/dt = kP(L - P) (capacity visible as the root of the second factor; the k differs by a factor of L from the other form), and dP/dt = 0.05P - 0.0001P² (expanded — factor it to find L: 0.05P(1 - P/500), capacity 500). Identifying L means finding the POSITIVE ROOT of the rate, whatever the packaging.

The equation's logic generalizes: any rate of the form P·(decreasing function hitting zero at L) produces ceiling-limited growth. The logistic is the simplest such model — quadratic rate, symmetric rise — which is exactly why it is the teachable, testable representative of the family.
key_terms: dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L): exponential early, choked near the ceiling
The positive root of the rate — attracting equilibrium, long-run limit
boxes: ap_alert

Given an expanded logistic rate like dP/dt = 0.08P - 0.002P², FACTOR before anything else: 0.08P(1 - P/40) reveals L = 40. Every subsequent question (limit, fastest growth at L/2) reads from the factored form; the expanded form hides both answers.

sections.title: Fastest Growth at Half Capacity
sections.subtitle: The L/2 property and the S-curve
sections.body:
The growth rate g(P) = kP(1 - P/L) is a downward parabola in P with roots at 0 and L — maximized at the vertex, P = L/2. The population grows FASTEST at exactly half capacity: below it, too few individuals to multiply quickly; above it, too little room. The L/2 fact is the BC exam's most reliable logistic question, asked as 'for what value of P is dP/dt greatest?'

The same point is the solution curve's INFLECTION: while P < L/2, growth accelerates (P' increasing, P'' > 0, concave up); past L/2, growth continues but decelerates (concave down). The S-curve's waist sits at height L/2 — Unit 5's epidemic chapter described this shape; the logistic equation is its engine. Concavity questions resolve by comparing P to L/2: 'P(0) = 30, L = 100 — is the curve concave up at the start?' Yes: 30 < 50.

The certified computation, for FRQs demanding it: P'' = d/dt[kP(1 - P/L)] = k(1 - 2P/L)·P' (chain rule on P). Since P' > 0 for 0 < P < L, the sign of P'' is the sign of (1 - 2P/L): positive below L/2, negative above — the parabola-vertex argument, formalized. Either justification earns the point; the differentiation route is the one to produce when 'use calculus' appears in the stem.

Maximum RATE versus maximum POPULATION is the planted confusion: the rate peaks at L/2; the population itself approaches (never attains) its supremum L. 'When is the population largest?' has no finite answer — it grows forever toward L; 'when is it growing fastest?' answers P = L/2. Reading which superlative the question asks is the entire trap.
key_terms: dP/dt is maximized at P = L/2 — the rate parabola's vertex
Concave up below L/2, down above: the S-curve's shape, certified by P''
Fastest growth at L/2; the population itself only approaches L
boxes: ap_alert

'For what P is the population growing fastest?' — L/2, by the vertex of the rate parabola, and the value of that fastest rate is k(L/2)(1/2) = kL/4. Both the location AND the maximal rate are one-line answers once the factored form is in hand.

sections.title: The Solution Formula
sections.subtitle: P = L/(1 + Ae^{-kt}), and where it comes from
sections.body:
Separating the logistic runs through Unit 6's partial fractions: dP/(P(1 - P/L)) = k dt decomposes (the chapter-7 FRQ previewed it), integrates to ln|P/(L - P)| = kt + C, and exponentiates to the standard form P(t) = L/(1 + Ae^{-kt}), where A = (L - P₀)/P₀ from the initial condition. BC exams have asked the full derivation rarely; they ask USE of the form regularly — and the derivation's existence is why the formula may be cited.

Reading the formula confirms every qualitative fact: at t = 0, P = L/(1 + A) = P₀ ✓; as t → ∞, e^{-kt} → 0 and P → L ✓; the curve rises monotonically between. The constant A encodes the start: large A (small P₀) means a long lag before the S rises; A near 0 (P₀ near L) means starting almost full.

Worked fit: L = 1000, P₀ = 100 gives A = (1000 - 100)/100 = 9: P = 1000/(1 + 9e^{-kt}). If additionally P(2) = 250: 250 = 1000/(1 + 9e^{-2k}) ⟹ 1 + 9e^{-2k} = 4 ⟹ e^{-2k} = 1/3 ⟹ k = (ln 3)/2. Finished model: P = 1000/(1 + 9·3^{-t/2}). Time-to-half-capacity then solves 500 = P(t): 1 + 9e^{-kt} = 2, e^{-kt} = 1/9, t = ln 9/k = 2·ln9/ln3 = 4 — clean by design, as exam numbers are.

The formula-versus-equation division of labor: limits, equilibria, fastest growth, concavity — from the EQUATION, no formula needed. Specific times and populations — from the FORMULA. FRQs braid both; answering equation-questions with formula algebra wastes minutes, and the strongest scripts visibly switch tools by sub-question.
key_terms: P = L/(1 + Ae^{-kt}), A = (L - P₀)/P₀ — derived via partial fractions
Large A: long low start; small A: begins near capacity
Equation for behavior; formula for specific times and values
boxes: ap_alert

Check P₀ against the formula instantly: P(0) = L/(1 + A). Given P = 2000/(1 + 24e^{-0.5t}), the initial population is 2000/25 = 80 and the capacity is 2000 — two answers read in five seconds from the shape alone.

sections.title: The Logistic Battery
sections.subtitle: Every question the AP asks, in one place
sections.body:
Given any logistic setup, the battery: (1) Carrying capacity? The positive root of the rate / the numerator of the solution form. (2) lim t→∞ P? L, for any P₀ > 0. (3) Where is growth fastest? P = L/2, rate kL/4. (4) Concave up/down at a given P? Compare to L/2. (5) Initial population? Evaluate the form at t = 0. (6) Specific times? Solve the formula with logs. Six questions, six one-line procedures — the chapter in a box.

Behavior from ABOVE capacity rounds out the picture: P₀ > L makes (1 - P/L) negative — the population FALLS toward L, concave up the whole descent (no inflection: the L/2 crossing never happens from above). Sketches starting above the ceiling decay smoothly onto it; the exam includes this branch in slope-field and sketch questions to catch students who memorized only the S.

Notation variants to absorb without flinching: y for P, M or K for L, logistic in 'proportional to both y and M - y' verbal dress. The verbal version — 'spreads at a rate proportional to the product of those infected and those not yet infected' — IS dP/dt = kP(M - P): rumor and epidemic models, the logistic's natural habitat.

Where it sits in the course: the logistic closes the DE unit by spending every tool — equilibria (ch 1), fields and no-crossing (ch 2), Euler when asked (ch 3), separation + partial fractions (ch 4, Unit 6), exponential limiting behavior (ch 5). One equation, the whole unit's machinery. Unit 8 turns back to integrals and their geometry; the DE toolkit returns on the exam braided into everything.
key_terms: Capacity, limit, fastest growth, concavity, initial value, time solves
P₀ > L: monotone decay onto the ceiling, concave up, no inflection
'Proportional to the product of P and (M - P)' — epidemics and rumors
boxes: ap_alert

The from-above branch (P₀ > L) has NO inflection point — the curve never crosses L/2. 'Find the inflection of the solution with P(0) = 1.5L' is a trick: the correct answer is that there isn't one, and the L/2 reflex without the P₀ check walks into it.

mcq.question: For dP/dt = 0.06P(1 - P/800) with P(0) = 50, lim t→∞ P(t) =
mcq.explanation: Positive start, attracting ceiling: the population converges to the carrying capacity 800.

mcq.question: The population governed by dP/dt = 0.06P(1 - P/800) grows fastest when P =
mcq.explanation: The rate parabola peaks at half capacity: L/2 = 400.

mcq.question: dP/dt = 0.1P - 0.0005P². The carrying capacity is
mcq.explanation: Factor: 0.1P(1 - P/200) — the positive root of the rate is L = 200.

mcq.question: P(t) = 600/(1 + 11e^{-0.4t}). The initial population is
mcq.explanation: P(0) = 600/(1 + 11) = 50. The numerator 600 is the capacity.

mcq.question: A logistic population starts at P(0) = 0.3L. At that moment the solution curve is
mcq.explanation: Below L: growing. Below L/2: growth still accelerating — concave up. The inflection waits at L/2.

frq.question:
A lake's fish population satisfies dP/dt = 0.5P(1 - P/2000), P(0) = 200, t in years.
(a) State the carrying capacity and lim t→∞ P(t), with a one-sentence justification from the equation.
(b) Find the population at which the growth rate is maximal, and compute that maximal rate.
(c) Is the solution curve concave up or down when P = 1500? Justify using the relationship between P and L/2.
rubric: (a) L = 2000; limit 2000 — positive rate on (0, 2000) drives P up toward the attracting equilibrium
(c) 1500 > L/2 = 1000: past the inflection — concave down
Justifications reference the equation's structure, not the formula
frq.model_answer: (a) The rate vanishes at P = 0 and P = 2000: carrying capacity L = 2000. Since dP/dt > 0 for 0 < P < 2000 and the population starts at 200, P increases toward the attracting equilibrium: lim t→∞ P = 2000. (b) The rate kP(1 - P/L) is a downward parabola in P maximized at L/2 = 1000 fish, where dP/dt = 0.5(1000)(1 - 1/2) = 250 fish per year. (c) At P = 1500 the population has passed L/2 = 1000, so the growth rate is now declining: P'' < 0 — the curve is concave down, in the flattening upper arm of the S.

frq.question:
A rumor spreads through a school of 1200 students at a rate proportional to the product of the number who have heard it and the number who have not. Initially 60 students have heard it.
(a) Write the differential equation, defining your constant.
(b) The solution has the form N = 1200/(1 + Ae^{-1200kt}). Find A from the initial condition.
(c) When 300 students have heard the rumor, is the rumor spreading at an increasing or decreasing rate? When 900 have heard it? Justify both.
rubric: (a) dN/dt = kN(1200 - N), k > 0 a proportionality constant
(c) Inflection at 600: at N = 300 < 600, rate increasing; at N = 900 > 600, rate decreasing
Justification via the L/2 threshold (or sign of N'')
frq.model_answer: (a) dN/dt = kN(1200 - N) with k > 0 — the verbal 'product of heard and not-heard' translated directly. (b) N(0) = 1200/(1 + A) = 60, so 1 + A = 20 and A = 19. (c) The spreading rate kN(1200 - N) peaks at half the school: N = 600. At N = 300 (below the waist), each new hearer accelerates the spread — the rate is still increasing (curve concave up). At N = 900 (above the waist), unheard students are scarce — the rate is decreasing (concave down). The rumor's fastest hour is the moment exactly half the school knows.

frq.question:
A logistic model has solution P(t) = 1000/(1 + 9e^{-kt}) with P(2) = 250, t in days.
(a) Verify that the initial population is 100, and find k exactly.
(b) Find the time at which the population reaches half its carrying capacity.
(c) A second population follows the SAME equation but starts at P(0) = 1250. Describe its behavior for t > 0 — monotonicity, concavity, and limit — and state whether it ever passes an inflection point.
rubric: (c) From above: decreasing, concave up, limit 1000
No inflection — the curve never crosses L/2 = 500 from above
frq.model_answer: (a) P(0) = 1000/(1 + 9) = 100 ✓. From P(2) = 250: 1 + 9e^{-2k} = 4, e^{-2k} = 1/3, so k = (ln 3)/2 per day. (b) Half capacity is 500: 1 + 9e^{-kt} = 2 gives e^{-kt} = 1/9, t = ln 9/k = (2 ln 9)/(ln 3) = 4 days. (c) Starting at 1250 > L = 1000, the factor (1 - P/L) is negative: the population DECREASES toward the ceiling, with lim t→∞ P = 1000. Its rate's magnitude shrinks as P nears L, so the descent flattens — concave up throughout. It never passes an inflection: inflections live at L/2 = 500, and this branch never goes below 1000, let alone 500.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Differential Equations on the AP Exam
hook: One unit, five instruments: translate, field, step, separate, and analyze. The exam braids them into single FRQs — this closing chapter is the rehearsal room where you run the full program on complete, exam-shaped problems.
learning_objectives: Recognize the standard DE FRQ architectures and their part-by-part rubrics
Switch fluently among field sketching, Euler stepping, and exact solving
Answer behavior questions from the equation when no solution is required
Avoid the unit's recurring deductions: lost constants, missing branches, unverified forms
Allocate time by recognizing which parts need formulas and which don't

sections.title: The Three FRQ Architectures
sections.subtitle: Know the building before entering
sections.body:
DE free-response questions arrive in three layouts. Architecture A — the braid: (a) slope field dashes, (b) tangent-line or Euler estimate, (c) separate and solve exactly. Architecture B — the model: (a) translate words to a DE, (b) behavior analysis (equilibria, limits, concavity) from the equation, (c) solve and predict. Architecture C — the logistic special: capacity, limits, L/2, concavity — often with NO solving at all.

Knowing the architecture sets time allocation. In A, part (c) carries the most points and the most algebra — budget for it. In B, the middle part is often answerable in two sentences from the equation; overworking it starves part (c). In C, the entire question may be equation-reading: students who launch into partial fractions on a question that never asks for P(t) burn ten minutes for zero additional points.

The parts interlock deliberately: part (b)'s Euler estimate should be CONSISTENT with part (a)'s field (stepping in the dashes' directions), and part (c)'s exact solution evaluated at the estimate's x should land near it (same side as concavity predicts). Cross-checking across parts catches errors while they're still fixable — the braid is also a built-in answer key.

Calculator policy shapes the work: DE FRQs appear in both sections. Calculator-active versions expect numeric integration or evaluation; no-calculator versions keep numbers humane (halves, small logs). The architecture is identical; only the arithmetic's outsourcing changes.
key_terms: Points concentrate in the solve for A, spread evenly for B, avoid solving in C
Field, estimate, and exact solution must agree — a free self-check
boxes: ap_alert

Read ALL parts of a DE FRQ before starting (a): if part (c) never asks for an explicit solution, the question is equation-analysis throughout, and any separation work is unpaid labor. The thirty-second preview sets the whole question's strategy.

sections.title: The Deduction Catalog
sections.subtitle: Where points actually die
sections.body:
Unit-wide bookkeeping of the recurring deductions, each with its prevention. Lost +C: the constant must appear at the moment of integration, not retrofitted. Late or missing initial-condition application: pin C on the implicit line. Missing ± / branch choice: after exponentiating logs or taking square roots, the initial condition's SIGN selects, and the selection is stated. Lost equilibria: dividing by h(y) requires either noting h's roots or checking the anchor isn't one.

Form-specific deductions: Euler tables missing the DE-evaluated slope column (method point gone); slope fields with uniform-tilt dashes (construction points gone); 'lim = L' answers without the positive-start hypothesis acknowledged when the stem makes it matter; separation shown without the actual SEPARATED LINE visible (the first rubric point of every solve).

Verification-question deductions: computing only one side of the DE, or substituting the solution into itself. Concavity deductions: asserting the S-curve shape without the P-versus-L/2 comparison or the P'' computation. Domain deductions: reporting a solution formula whose denominator dies inside the claimed interval.

The catalog compresses to one habit: make every move VISIBLE — the separated line, the constant's birth, the condition's application, the branch's selection, both sides of every verification. DE rubrics are checklists of visible moves; invisible correct work and visible correct work score differently, and only one of them scores fully.
key_terms: C born at integration, pinned at the implicit stage, never retrofitted
± after exponentiation, root choice by the anchor — stated, not implied
DE rubrics check moves; work done invisibly earns invisibly
boxes: ap_alert

The five-second pre-submission audit for any DE solve: separated line visible? C present and pinned? Branch stated? Equilibrium checked? Domain sane? Five checks, five of the unit's most common deductions neutralized.

sections.title: Worked Composite One
sections.subtitle: Architecture A, executed in full
sections.body:
The problem: dy/dx = y²(1 + x), with the points (0, 1) marked on a grid. (a) Sketch dashes at (0, ±1), (1, ±1), (-1, ±1). (b) Tangent-line estimate of y(0.2) for the solution through (0, 1). (c) Solve exactly with y(0) = 1 and compute y(0.2).

(a): slopes are y²(1 + x): at (0, ±1): 1 and 1 (y² kills sign); at (1, ±1): 2, 2; at (-1, ±1): 0, 0 — vertical line x = -1 carries flat dashes. Note y² makes the field symmetric in y: dashes above and below the axis match. (b): slope at (0,1) is 1: y(0.2) ≈ 1 + 0.2 = 1.2. (c): separate: y^{-2} dy = (1 + x) dx; integrate: -1/y = x + x²/2 + C; pin: -1 = C. Solve: y = 1/(1 - x - x²/2). Evaluate: y(0.2) = 1/(1 - 0.2 - 0.02) = 1/0.78 ≈ 1.282.

The cross-check in action: 1.2 (tangent) versus 1.282 (exact) — the estimate ran LOW, consistent with concavity: y'' = 2y y'(1+x) + y² > 0 near the anchor (everything positive), concave up, tangent lines undershoot. All three parts cohere; an estimate of 1.4 or an exact value below 1.2 would have flagged an error somewhere.

Domain coda, the strongest finish: the solution lives while 1 - x - x²/2 > 0, i.e., up to the positive root x = √3 - 1 ≈ 0.732 — a finite-time blowup invisible in the original equation and revealed by the solve. Solutions of innocent-looking DEs can have short lives; the formula knows.
key_terms: Field mechanics, tangent estimate, separation — one problem, three instruments
Estimate vs exact vs concavity: all three must tell one story
Solutions can die at algebraic walls the equation never advertised

After solving exactly, ALWAYS evaluate at the estimate's x and compare: same side as concavity predicts, reasonable gap. Thirty seconds, and it has caught sign errors, dropped constants, and wrong branches on countless real exam papers.

sections.title: Worked Composite Two and the Unit's Exit
sections.subtitle: Architecture B, then the road ahead
sections.body:
The problem: 'Oxygen dissolves into a tank of water at a rate proportional to the difference between the saturation level 12 mg/L and the current concentration y.' y(0) = 3. (a) Write the DE. (b) Without solving: equilibrium, monotonicity, concavity, limit. (c) Solve; find when y = 9.

(a): dy/dt = k(12 - y), k > 0 — cooling's twin with a positive gap. (b): equilibrium y = 12; for y < 12 the rate is positive — increasing; differentiating, y'' = -k y' < 0 — concave down (rising, flattening); lim t→∞ y = 12. Four facts, zero solving — the part (b) discipline. (c): separate dy/(12 - y) = k dt: -ln|12 - y| = kt + C; pin at (0, 3): C = -ln 9. Solve: 12 - y = 9e^{-kt}, y = 12 - 9e^{-kt}. When y = 9: 9e^{-kt} = 3, t = (ln 3)/k.

Note what part (c) left symbolic: without a second data point, k stays a letter and the answer is (ln 3)/k — fully acceptable, and a reminder that 'solve' means 'express,' not 'decimalize.' Had the stem supplied y(2) = 7 — then 9e^{-2k} = 5 pins k = (1/2)ln(9/5), and the time becomes 2 ln 3/ln(9/5).

The unit's exit interview: you can now read a rate sentence into an equation, see every solution at once in a field, walk one numerically, name the nameable ones by separation, and extract behavior — equilibria, limits, concavity, inflections — straight from the equation. Unit 8 returns to accumulation with geometry (areas, volumes, arc length); the DE instruments rest until the exam reassembles them. They will reassemble.
key_terms: dy/dt = k(L_sat - y): cooling's structure, rising flavor
Equilibrium, monotonicity, concavity, limit — all pre-formula
boxes: ap_alert

When a model has an unspecified k and the question asks for a time, the answer SHOULD contain k — e.g., t = (ln 3)/k. Inventing a value or refusing to answer are both wrong; symbolic answers in stated constants are complete and earn full credit.

mcq.question: An FRQ part asks only: 'Find lim t→∞ P(t) for the solution of dP/dt = 0.2P(1 - P/600) with P(0) = 50.' The most efficient correct response is

choices.A: 600, because P starts in (0, 600) where the rate is positive and 600 is the attracting equilibrium
choices.B: the full solution P(t) followed by the limit
choices.C: an Euler approximation with small h

mcq.explanation: Equation-reading answers limit questions; solving is unpaid labor. (D confuses the rate's decline with the population's.)

mcq.question: After integrating a separated equation to ln|y| = x² + C with y(0) = -4, the correct next move is

choices.A: |y| = e^C e^{x²}, so y = Ae^{x²} with A = ±e^C; the condition gives A = -4
choices.B: y = e^{x² + C} and C = ln 4

mcq.explanation: The ± consolidation lets A be negative — required here. B and D force positive y and lose the sign.

mcq.question: For dy/dx = x - y², which task can be completed exactly with this unit's tools?

choices.A: an Euler approximation of y(1) from y(0) = 0
choices.C: the general solution in elementary functions

mcq.explanation: x - y² doesn't factor by variable: not separable. But Euler (and fields) need no formula — exactly their purpose.

mcq.explanation: The anchor's negative sign selects the negative branch — and stating the selection is part of the answer.

mcq.question: An Euler estimate gives y(1) ≈ 2.0; the exact solve gives y(1) = 1.7; the computed y'' is positive on the interval. This combination

choices.A: signals an error: concave up predicts the Euler estimate should be BELOW the exact value
choices.C: shows the exact solution is wrong by definition

mcq.explanation: Concave up ⟹ chords undershoot ⟹ Euler low. An overshooting Euler with positive y'' means one of the three computations is wrong — the cross-check did its job.

frq.question:
Consider dy/dx = y²(1 + x) with the initial condition y(0) = 1.
(a) On the axes provided, sketch the field's segments at the six points (0, ±1), (1, ±1), (-1, ±1), and state the field's symmetry in y.
(b) Use a tangent-line approximation to estimate y(0.2).
(c) Solve the IVP exactly, evaluate y(0.2), and reconcile the comparison with the solution's concavity near x = 0.
rubric: (a) Slopes 1, 1, 2, 2, 0, 0 at the six points; y² makes dashes mirror across the x-axis
Reconciliation: y'' > 0 near 0 ⟹ tangent underestimates ⟹ 1.2 < 1.282 ✓
frq.model_answer: (a) Slope = y²(1 + x): at (0, ±1): 1 and 1; at (1, ±1): 2 and 2; at (-1, ±1): 0 and 0. Because y enters only as y², the field is symmetric across the x-axis — mirrored points carry identical dashes. (b) y(0.2) ≈ y(0) + 0.2·y'(0) = 1 + 0.2(1) = 1.2. (c) Separate: y^{-2} dy = (1 + x) dx; integrate: -1/y = x + x²/2 + C; y(0) = 1 pins C = -1. So y = 1/(1 - x - x²/2), and y(0.2) = 1/(1 - 0.2 - 0.02) = 1/0.78 ≈ 1.282. Reconciliation: y'' = 2yy'(1 + x) + y² is positive near (0, 1) (all factors positive) — concave up — so the tangent line undershoots, exactly as 1.2 < 1.282 shows.

frq.question:
Oxygen dissolves into a tank at a rate proportional to the difference between the saturation concentration 12 mg/L and the current concentration y(t); y(0) = 3.
(a) Write the differential equation.
(b) WITHOUT solving, find the equilibrium, determine the solution's monotonicity and concavity for 3 ≤ y < 12, and state lim t→∞ y.
(c) Solve the equation, and find the time at which y = 9 in terms of the constant k.
rubric: (a) dy/dt = k(12 - y), k > 0
(b) Equilibrium 12; increasing (rate > 0 below 12); y'' = -k·y' < 0: concave down; limit 12
Symbolic-k answer presented as complete
frq.model_answer: (a) dy/dt = k(12 - y) with k > 0. (b) The rate vanishes at y = 12: the equilibrium. For y < 12 the rate is positive, so the concentration increases. Differentiating: y'' = -k·y' < 0 (since y' > 0): concave down — rising steeply at first, flattening toward saturation. lim t→∞ y = 12. (c) Separate: dy/(12 - y) = k dt; -ln|12 - y| = kt + C; at (0, 3): C = -ln 9. Then 12 - y = 9e^{-kt}, so y = 12 - 9e^{-kt}. Setting y = 9: 9e^{-kt} = 3, e^{-kt} = 1/3, t = (ln 3)/k — complete as a symbolic answer since the stem provides no second data point to pin k.

frq.question:
A disease spreads through a town of 5000 according to dI/dt = kI(5000 - I), where I(t) is the number infected, I(0) = 100, and the infection is observed spreading fastest on day 14.
(a) What is the number of infected people on day 14? Justify.
(b) Sketch-describe the graph of I: concavity regions, the inflection, and the limit.
(c) Public health intervention will begin when 4000 are infected. Will the rate of new infections at that moment be larger or smaller than at day 14? Compute the ratio of the two rates.
rubric: (a) Fastest spread at half the town: I = 2500 on day 14 (L/2 property)
(b) Concave up to day 14 (I < 2500), inflection at (14, 2500), concave down after; lim = 5000
Smaller at 4000 — 64% of the peak rate
frq.model_answer: (a) The logistic rate kI(5000 - I) peaks when I = 5000/2 = 2500. 'Spreading fastest on day 14' therefore means I(14) = 2500 people. (b) The curve rises from 100, concave up while I < 2500 (accelerating spread), inflects at the point (14, 2500), then continues rising concave down (decelerating spread), approaching the ceiling: lim t→∞ I = 5000 — the full S. (c) Rate at I = 4000: k(4000)(1000) = 4,000,000k. Rate at the peak: k(2500)(2500) = 6,250,000k. Ratio: 4,000,000/6,250,000 = 16/25 = 0.64. The intervention begins when new infections run at only 64% of their day-14 peak — smaller, because 4000 is well past the half-town inflection.
